title: Graceful degrade routing playbook
content:
Context and goal:

This is a working playbook for how the Redwood control plane should make real-time routing + fallback decisions when serving inference traffic across model variants, capacity tiers, and regions. The core goal is to preserve availability and acceptable latency under partial failures or constrained capacity while minimizing cost and avoiding catastrophic quality regressions for customer workloads.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted API + Dedicated routing layers; private deployments should be able to opt into the same policies if desired.
- We assume: model catalog contains multiple compatible variants (e.g., base, quantized-4, distill-small) with known performance/quality profiles.
- Tiers: Premium (reserved/dedicated), Standard (shared-hosted), Spot/Burst. Regions have different latency/cost characteristics.
- Customers can configure SLOs (latency percentile), cost-sensitivity, and quality minimums (e.g., minimum perplexity change or eval score).

High-level decision flow (textual pseudograph):
1) Request arrives -> lookup customer policy (SLO, cost-preference, allowed fallbacks) -> query region affinity + availability map -> pick primary node pool (preferred region + tier).
2) If primary pool has capacity and model variant available -> route.
3) If primary pool busy or degraded -> evaluate fallback candidates ranked by: 1) SLO impact (latency increase), 2) quality delta, 3) cost delta, 4) regional affinity (legal/data residency).
4) If acceptable candidate exists -> route with chosen model variant + add request metadata (fallback_reason, candidate_rank).
5) If no acceptable candidate -> apply graceful degradation strategies: one or more of 
   - reduce request concurrency / shed non-critical requests 
   - apply cached responses or partial results (if applicable) 
   - respond with structured error that includes retry-after and degrade_options header

Ranking heuristics for candidates (weights are tunable):
- Latency penalty (p50/p95 change relative to SLO): weight 4
- Estimated quality delta (based on evals for the workload profile): weight 5
- Cost delta per-token: weight 2
- Data residency compliance: hard constraint (exclude if violates)
- Customer preference (explicit allow/block for quantized/cheap variants): override weights

Model variant catalog metadata (must exist for each model):
- variant_id (string)
- size/architecture info (string)
- qps_per_gpu_estimate (string)
- latency_profile_by_seq (string)
- eval_score_by_prompt_set (string)
- cost_per_token_estimate (string)
- compatibility_tags (list of strings)
- allowed_for_tiers (list of strings)

Tiered capacity behavior (practical rules):
- Premium: guaranteed capacity. Only route to lower tiers if explicitly allowed by customer policy or Premium pool unhealthy.
- Standard: default for new/unaffiliated traffic. Can overflow to Burst if under heavy load.
- Spot/Burst: best-effort; use for non-critical background jobs, batch requests, or when customer has cost-first preference.
- When saturating a pool, trigger progressive spillover steps: 1) soft-throttle best-effort routes, 2) shift to compatible model variants in same region, 3) cross-region spillover to nearest acceptable region, 4) fall back to lower-quality variant in same/different region.

Regional spillover policy details:
- Primary preference: keep within customer's configured home region. If home region capacity < threshold (configurable, default 20% spare headroom) then consider nearest regions in latency-sorted order.
- Geo-legal blocker: if a customer has residence constraint, mark regions as forbidden and exclude in ranking.
- Inter-region spillover includes an added latency penalty estimate; must still meet customer's p95 SLO unless customer explicitly allows p99 expansion.
- Cost accounting: traffic moved cross-region should show a cost metric and signal to billing/optimization pipelines.

Graceful degradation modes (ordered from least to most invasive):
1) Adaptive batching increase with latency-aware caps (slightly increase effective latency to reduce cost and keep tokens flowing).
2) Prefix KV-cache replay for common completions (serve cached continuation when quality delta small).
3) Quantized or distilled model variants with explicit quality warnings in response headers.
4) Function-calling only mode (disallow freeform generation for highest-fidelity structured tasks).
5) Queue with ETA (return 202 + retry-after) or synchronous partial result + background completion webhook.
6) Best-effort error with degrade-reason and suggested next steps.

Telemetry and observability requirements (what we must emit):
- per-request: chosen_region, chosen_tier, model_variant, fallback_reason (none|capacity|error|policy), candidate_list_scores, final_score, routed_latency_estimate, served_latency, and cache_hit boolean.
- per-policy metrics: fallbacks_count, spillovers_by_region, degrade_mode_incidents, quality_regressions_by_prompt_set.
- SLO alerting: when fallbacks cause p95/p99 to exceed configured thresholds for a customer for more than X minutes, page on-call and create auto-ticket.

Safety and quality guardrails:
- Require an explicit "allowed_fallbacks" flag for each customer that lists acceptable variant tags (e.g., allow-quantized, allow-distill). Default is conservative: only same-family variants.
- For any variant that may introduce >5% eval regression on a monitored prompt set, require a canary rollout: route <=2% traffic initially with automatic rollback if metric delta > threshold.
- Function call and tool-interfaces are treated as critical: avoid degrading them unless severe outage.

Implementation notes for control plane engineers:
- Keep decision logic side-effect-free: compute candidate ranking then execute routing in atomic step to avoid double-booking GPUs.
- Maintain a real-time availability map derived from serving runtime heartbeats + queue depths + GPU load and memory pressure signals.
- Use a small decision engine component (stateless) that reads availability map + policy store and emits route directives. Keep it horizontally scalable and cacheable.
- Store policy + allowed_fallbacks in customer config service; expose a dry-run endpoint for simulating fallback decisions for specific traffic patterns.

Operational runbook (short):
- If "cascade fallback" alert fires: check primary region GPUs metric > 90% and error rates. If network partition to region, enable pre-baked cross-region spillover rule for affected customer cohorts.
- If quality regression alarms on an evaluation set: identify which fallback variant was the majority contributor, rollback that variant for affected customers, and create incident to retrain/evaluate variant.
- For persistent capacity shortage: evaluate capacity autoscaling thresholds for Dedicated pools and propose reserve expansion (billing lead + account owner informed).

Open questions and TODOs:
- How to represent multi-model requests (tool calling that touches multiple variants) in ranking? TODO: define composite score function.
- Explore probabilistic hedging: send to two variants and accept earliest? (costly) TODO: prototype for high-SLO customers.
- Decide default allowed_fallbacks for free-tier customers (cost vs. availability tradeoff).
- Build a lightweight simulator to replay historical traffic and measure fallback frequency before changing warn/thresholds.

Appendix: quick checklist for new model onboarding to be used in fallback decisions:
- Provide latency-by-seqlen histogram (p50/p95/p99)
- Provide eval deltas per canonical prompt sets (small numeric summary)
- Tag model compatibility (chat, embeddings, code)
- Define allowed_tiers and region availability

Notes-to-self / rough ideas:
- Consider a per-customer hysteresis window to avoid flip-flopping between regions when capacity fluctuates rapidly.
- Expose explanation metadata in API responses to help SREs and customers debug fallbacks (but keep terse).
- We might want to expose a "graceful-mode" toggle at account level so that platform triggers more aggressive cost-saving fallbacks during corporate run-outs (e.g., end-of-quarter).

End of draft.

Feedback welcome — particularly from serving-runtime (evan), SRE (luis) and product (priya) on matching the policy UX to what billing and support need.
